title.narrative: Aggressive Infection Related East Africa Lymphoma

description.narrative: Evaluation and Transfer of mobile whole slide tissue scanners and liquidbiopsies to deliver fast and precise diagnosis for improved outcomes of children and young adults with EBV-driven lymphoma: a joint Tanzanian and UgandanPaediatric Oncology Network Initiative

Summary:Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is facing a major public health challenge from non-communicable diseases. Thedisease burden attributable to cancer is rapidly rising, with a predicted 85% increase in incidence by2030. In a region where 40% of the entire population is under the age of 15, cancer is more likely topresent in younger patients in sub-Saharan Africa, evidenced by a rising paediatric/adolescentincidence.Aggressive lymphoma accounts for nearly 10% of all cancer diagnosis in the region, due to a strongassociation with Epstein Barr virus (EBV) infection(5,7,8). Despite established diagnostic pathways,treatments and improving outcomes in developed countries, diagnostics, treatment and support areseverely limited in SSA and outcomes poor(2,9,10). Tissue diagnosis in particular poses a significant challenge with a single pathologist being responsible for millions of patients within a region(9).Furthermore, there are significant practical challenges to obtaining tumour tissue from children.With the availability of digital pathology and low-cost peripheral blood DNA analysis, we now havethe potential to rapidly and accurately screen, diagnose and monitor children and young adults withEBV associated lymphoma (EBVL) without the specific need for tissue biopsy. We already havepreliminary results from our laboratory demonstrating high sensitivity and specificity of this methodfor lymphoma diagnosis(11).This liquid biopsy only requires an additional 4-10ml (1-3 teaspoons) of peripheral venous blood collectedinto a specified blood tube. Given that all patients currently have standard of care (SOC) testing, includingroutine blood tests and often an insertion of a long-term venous access line, this additional sample posesminimal if any risk to the patient.Our proposal also aims to address issues surrounding pathological diagnosis. Currently in East Africa,a single pathologist is responsible for 3.2m patients. Thus, despite tissue biopsy remaining as the goldstandard diagnostic test, a major hurdle to diagnosis is obtaining a result in a timely manner. Samplesare often transported overseas for reporting in large established tertiary labs.We will therefore assess the utility of a digital microscopy platform which we are already using for teachingand training in the region. This technology will enable local scientists of obtain diagnostic quality digitalimages of traditional histopathology glass slides that can be shared immediately for reporting.In collaboration with our partners across SSA, we will assess the accuracy of these two low cost noveltechnologies for diagnosing EBVL in East African patients aged 5 to 21 suspected of having the condition.Technology 1: Liquid biopsy – detection of fragments of lymphoma specific DNA shed into the peripheralblood from tumours. Also known as circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA). Testing requires collection of 10ml(2 teaspoons) or peripheral blood. We already have pilot data in an Oxford cohort of lymphoma patientsthat demonstrates a high sensitivity and specificity for ctDNA as a diagnostic tool.Technology 2: Mobile digital microscopy – device that can reproduce high-resolution, diagnosticquality, whole slide digital images from blood smears and tissue biopsy slides.Aim: to improve diagnosis of childhood lymphoma in sub-Saharan Africa by making it faster and moreprecise using mobile digital pathology devices and liquid biopsyObjectives1. Assess the diagnostic accuracy of liquid biopsy testing2. Asses the diagnostic accuracy of digital pathology3. Development of a digital pathology machine learning algorithm4. Transfer of above novel tests and associated expertise to local laboratoriesPatients Children and adolescents aged 3 to 30 suspected of having EBVL.DesignRetrospective Case control study.MethodAll patients recruited will continue to have routine local standard of care testing.We will compare the two technologies against current local ‘gold standard’ tests for diagnosing EBVL.- Gold Standard tissue glass slide light-microscopy versus liquid biopsy (single blood test, 4-10ml at studyentry)- Gold Standard tissue glass slide light-microscopy versus whole slide digital images (WSI)The results of the novel tests will be analysed retrospectively, therefore therapeutic decisions will only bemade based upon the gold standard test results.Provided we observe a strong correlation between WSI, ctDNA and the gold standard test, we will plan toproceed to a second study where we will assess the time-to-diagnosis for these three methods.
